lessons.title: 人 (rén) — two strokes, and a person walking
lessons.gloss: person — the first character, and the shape of a walking figure

notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on, your eyes, for letter shapes on the page and your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script — the shape and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: You have heard Mandarin pitch. Now you meet the writing, and this book will hand it to you one piece at a time — never a character you have not been shown the parts of first.
This is the whole first piece:
人 (rén).
Two strokes. That is the entire character.
人 rén means person.

Look at it before you read another word about it. A stroke leaning down-left, a stroke leaning down-right, meeting at the top. It is a figure standing on two legs, seen from the side. You are not being asked to take that on faith — the oldest surviving forms of this character, scratched into ox bone three thousand years ago, are recognisably a standing person, and the two legs are the part that lasted.
Write it in this order, and the order is not a suggestion:
the left stroke, from the top down to the lower left — a falling sweep.
the right stroke, starting near the top of the first and pressing down to the lower right.
Left before right. Almost every character you meet will obey it, and it is worth meeting here — on a character with two strokes — rather than later on one with fifteen.
The pitch is second tone: rén rises, like the end of an English question.

segments.instruction: 人 — left stroke first, then right. Say rén as you finish it.
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: 人 — left stroke first, then right. Say *rén* as you finish it.]
[YOU SAY: **rén**, rising]

segments.text: Which stroke goes first — the one leaning left, or the one leaning right? (The left.)
Source: Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart; stroke order per the PRC standard Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan (1997).

segments.prompt: How many strokes does the character for 'person' have?

feedback.correct: Two — the left falling stroke, then the right.
feedback.incorrect: Two: one stroke down-left, one down-right.

lessons.title: 亻 (rén (as a component)) — the same person, standing sideways
lessons.gloss: the person component — 人 squashed upright to stand at a character's left edge

notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script — one character, two postures and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Write the two-stroke character for person once, from memory. Left stroke, then right.
Every Chinese character is written inside an evenly sized square block — whether it has two strokes or twenty, it occupies the same footprint. That one fact drives everything you are about to see.
Because when two pieces have to share a block, one of them must get out of the way. Here is what person looks like when it moves to the left edge to make room:
亻 (rén (as a component)).
Still two strokes. Still the same piece. But the wide-legged stance has been pulled upright into one short slant on top of one long vertical, narrow enough that something else can sit beside it.

This is not a different character. It is the same one, squashed. Chinese does this constantly, and the squashed forms are called components. When you see 亻 (rén (as a component)) at the left edge of a block, the character is telling you: this word is about a person.
Write it:
the short slant, down-left, at the top.
the long vertical, dropping from the middle of that slant.
Top before bottom — the second of the two rules.

segments.instruction: 人, then 亻 (rén (as a component)) beside it. Notice you did not learn a new piece — you learned a new posture.
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: 人, then 亻 beside it. Notice you did not learn a new piece — you learned a new **posture**.]

segments.instruction: 亻 (rén (as a component)) is tall and thin because it is only using the left half of its square.
segments.source: [YOU NOTICE: 亻 is tall and thin because it is only using the left half of its square.]

segments.text: Why does person change shape at all? (To leave room in the square for whatever stands beside it.)
Source: Unicode CJK Radicals Supplement chart; stroke order per the PRC standard Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan (1997).

segments.prompt: A character has the narrow upright person component at its left edge. What does that tell you about the word?

feedback.correct: Right — the left edge is carrying the meaning.
feedback.incorrect: It signals that the word has to do with a PERSON.

blocks.title: Script — the other kind of component

segments.text: So far a component has meant something: the person piece says this is about a person. Here is a component that works the other way.
尔 (ěr).
尔 ěr. Five strokes: a short slant across the top, a broad cover beneath it, then a small stroke each side of a central vertical that finishes with a hook.
Now the part that matters, and it is the single most useful fact about Chinese writing:

Most characters are built from one component pointing at the MEANING and another pointing at the SOUND. When 尔 turns up inside a character, it is usually there because the word sounds something like ěr — not because the word has anything to do with what 尔 means on its own.

That is a strange idea when your reading habits come from an alphabet, where every piece is sound and none is meaning. It is also a relief: it means characters are not arbitrary pictures to be memorised whole. They are built, from a small stock of pieces, and once you know the pieces you can often guess both halves of a character you have never seen.
The pitch is third tone: ěr dips low.

segments.instruction: 尔 (ěr) — top slant, cover, then the middle with its hook last
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: 尔 — top slant, cover, then the middle with its hook last]
[YOU SAY: **ěr**, low and dipping]

segments.text: Two kinds of component, then. One tells you what a word is about; the other tells you roughly how it sounds. Which kind is 尔 (ěr)?
Source: Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart; stroke order per the PRC standard Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan (1997).

segments.prompt: When a component is inside a character for its SOUND rather than its meaning, what is it telling you?
acceptedResponses: roughly how the word is pronounced

feedback.correct: Yes — it points at the pronunciation, not the meaning.
feedback.incorrect: It points at the PRONUNCIATION of the whole character.

lessons.title: Putting two pieces together — and reading the result
lessons.gloss: the first character you can read by assembling it — person on the left, sound on the right

notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on, your eyes, for letter shapes on the page and your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script — the assembly and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.source: [PAUSE 3s]

segments.text: Two pieces, both already yours. Draw them side by side:
亻 (rén (as a component)) 尔 (ěr).
The narrow person on the left. The five-stroke sound piece on the right.
Push them into one square block and you have written a character:
亻 (rén (as a component)) + 尔 (ěr) becomes 你 (nǐ).
Read it the way you now know how to read it, half at a time:
the left half is the person component. So this word is about a person.
the right half is the sound piece ěr. So this word sounds something like ěr.

The word is nǐ. And that is the honest state of the sound half — nǐ and ěr are close, not identical. A sound component gets you into the neighbourhood, not to the door. Sound components were chosen over two thousand years of pronunciation change, and the pronunciations moved out from under them. Expect a hint, and you will be right most of the time; expect a rule, and Chinese will embarrass you weekly.
Write it left before right, exactly as you learned each half:
亻 (rén (as a component)) — short slant, long vertical.
尔 (ěr) — top slant, cover, then the middle and its hook.
Seven strokes in total, and you did not memorise a single new one.
Stop and take the measure of what just happened, because it is the reason this book teaches script this way.

You have not been shown a picture and asked to remember it. You were given two pieces, one at a time, and then shown that a character is what you get when they share a square. The next character works the same way, and so does the one after that. There are only a few hundred components in common use, and they recombine — which is what makes several thousand characters a climb rather than a cliff.

segments.prompt: In this character, which half points at the MEANING — the left or the right?

feedback.incorrect: The LEFT half — the person component carries the meaning here.

lessons.title: 女 (nǚ) — three strokes, seated
lessons.gloss: woman — three strokes, and another figure that survived from the oracle bones

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script — the shape and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: One character so far assembles from two known halves. Draw it, and name each half as you write it.
A new piece, and like the first one it is old enough to still look like what it meant:
女 (nǚ).
女 nǚ — woman. Three strokes.

The oracle-bone form is a kneeling or seated figure with the arms crossed in front. The modern character keeps the crossing: that long horizontal running right across the middle is the arms, and the two curving strokes beneath and around it are the folded body. It has straightened out over three thousand years, but nothing has been added or taken away.
Write it in this order:
the stroke that starts upper-right and curves down and left.
the stroke that crosses it, going down-left then flicking right.
the long horizontal, last, sweeping across both.
That third stroke going last is worth noticing — a long horizontal that crosses everything else usually waits until the end.
The pitch is third tone, and the vowel is the rounded ü: say ee and then push your lips into a whistle without changing the tongue.

segments.instruction: 女 (nǚ) — and let the crossing bar go last
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: 女 — and let the crossing bar go last]

segments.instruction: nǚ, low and dipping, lips rounded
segments.source: [YOU SAY: **nǚ**, low and dipping, lips rounded]

segments.text: Which stroke comes last, and why? (The long horizontal — a bar that crosses the whole character usually waits.)
Source: Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart; stroke order per the PRC standard Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan (1997).

segments.prompt: How many strokes are in the character for 'woman'?

feedback.correct: Three, with the long crossing bar written last.
feedback.incorrect: Three — two curving strokes, then the long horizontal across them.

lessons.gloss: child — three strokes, a swaddled infant with its arms out

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Three strokes, crossing bar last. Draw the seated figure you met a moment ago.
子 (zǐ).
子 zǐ — child. Three strokes again, and again a figure you can still see once you are told where to look.

This one is an infant drawn from the front: a large head on top, two arms out to the sides, and the legs bound together so they read as one stroke rather than two. Babies were carried swaddled, and the character kept the bundle.
Write it:
the short stroke across the top, turning down — the head.
the vertical with a hook, dropping through the middle — the wrapped body.
the horizontal across the middle — the arms.
The pitch is third tone. The z is not the English z of zoo: it is the ds at the end of English beds, made with the tongue tip against the teeth.

segments.instruction: 子 (zǐ) — head, hooked body, then arms
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: 子 — head, hooked body, then arms]

segments.instruction: two characters now, both three strokes, both once pictures of people. Draw them side by side and compare which parts are curved.
segments.source: [YOU NOTICE: two characters now, both three strokes, both once pictures of people. Draw them side by side and compare which parts are curved.]

segments.text: The stroke that runs down the middle carries a hook. What part of the picture is it? (The wrapped body and legs.)
Source: Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart; stroke order per the PRC standard Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan (1997).

segments.source: [PAUSE 3s]

segments.text: Both pieces are yours. Draw them side by side:
女 (nǚ) 子 (zǐ).
Squeeze them into one block, woman on the left, child on the right:
女 (nǚ) + 子 (zǐ) becomes 好 (hǎo).
好 hǎo. Six strokes, three from each half, and again nothing new.

Note what is different about this assembly. The first one you built had a meaning half and a sound half. This one has two meaning halves and no sound half at all — neither piece sounds like hǎo. Both kinds of character are common, and you cannot tell which kind you are holding until you look.

When 女 (nǚ) is squeezed into the left of a block its long crossing bar stops short rather than sweeping past the middle, so as not to collide with what stands beside it. Same piece, narrower posture — the same accommodation you already saw the person component make.

blocks.title: What you've built — and a caution

segments.text: You will find it said that 好 (hǎo) means good because a woman with a child is a good thing.

Treat that as a story, not as evidence. It is memorable, it is repeated everywhere, and there is no agreement among specialists that it is what happened — competing accounts read the woman as the sound half in an older pronunciation, or read the pair as a woman caring for a child. This book will hand you an etymology when there is a source behind it and tell you plainly when there is not, and this is one of the second kind.
Use the pairing as a memory hook, which it genuinely is. Do not file it as a fact about why the word means what it means.

segments.instruction: 好 (hǎo) — the whole left half first, then the whole right half
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: 好 — the whole left half first, then the whole right half]

segments.instruction: the crossing bar on the left half no longer sweeps all the way across. Why not?
segments.source: [YOU NOTICE: the crossing bar on the left half no longer sweeps all the way across. Why not?]

segments.text: Six strokes, two pieces, and you built both pieces yourself. What is the one claim in this lesson you should NOT repeat as fact?
Source: Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart; stroke order per the PRC standard Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan (1997).

segments.prompt: Does this character have a component that points at its pronunciation?

feedback.correct: No — both halves carry meaning here.
feedback.incorrect: No. Both halves are meaning components; neither sounds like hǎo.
